newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba explains arrests of four dissidents.
newsitem.headline: Cuba explains arrests of four dissidents.

text.p: Cuba's Foreign Ministry has said four political dissidents detained last week are being held because they threatened foreign investors, lied about the economy and tried to disrupt upcoming elections.
The Cuban position was contained in a note, obtained by Reuters on Wednesday, responding to foreign expressions of concern.

European Union and Canadian diplomats in Havana met Cuban Foreign Ministry officials last Friday to convey their governments' "deep dismay and concern" over the July 16 arrests. EU diplomats called for the release of the four dissidents, three men and one woman, diplomatic sources said.

Last week, Cuban Foreign Ministry spokesman Miguel Alfonso said the four, members of a group calling itself the "Internal Dissidence Working Group", were being held in connection with "counter-revolutionary crimes." He gave no more details.

A Foreign Ministry note sent this week to at least one embassy that had inquired into the case gave details of the accusations faced by the four. But diplomatic sources said they understood they had still not yet been formally charged.

The July 22 diplomatic note said the detained -- Vladimiro Roca, Martha Beatriz Roque, Felix Bonne and Rene Gomez Manzano -- had been engaged in "intense activity aimed at subverting the legal and constitutional order of the Republic of Cuba."

It added that the authorities had proof that the dissidents had been seeking to disrupt local government elections scheduled for Oct. 19. Since May, the dissidents had held at least two public news conferences and in one they had called for a boycott of the upcoming one-party elections.

The Foreign Ministry note said the detained men had also released "false and inexact data" about the Cuban economy. Their intention was to "negatively influence internal and international public opinion and especially existing and potential partners and investors," the note added.
The dissidents were also accused of "threatening foreign businessmen who negotiate with Cuba, even raising the posibility of reprisals," the Foreign Ministry note said.

During one of their news conferences, the dissidents had shown reporters a letter from them to foreign businessmen warning them of the consequences of investing in Cuba under the current one-party Communist government.
"In all these activities, they (the dissidents) have had logistical support from officials of the U.S. Interests Section in Havana," the official note said, without elaborating.
It did not specifically link the detained dissidents to the explosion of two small bombs in two central Havana hotels last July 12. Three people were injured in the blasts.
But the note ended: "The Cuban authorities have sufficient proof of the involvement of these citizens with leaders of terrorist groups based in the territory of the United States."

Cuban authorities have made clear that they believe right- wing anti-Communist Cuban exiles in Miami are behind the recent bomb blasts, which Cuban officials say appear aimed at damaging the island's growing tourist industry.
The U.S. government has asked Cuba to provide evidence to support an initial accusation that the people and materials involved in the bombings came from the United States.

Diplomatic sources said the four were being held at Villa Marista, the headquarters of Cuba's state security services. The Foreign Ministry note did not say if or when the detained dissidents would be brought to trial.
